title: One replacement, every tool
summary: The same rewrite in JavaScript, Python, sed, VS Code and Rider, case conversion in the editor, and real refactors: rename a field, swap arguments, add global usings.

steps.title: Same idea, different spelling
body: Every tool has a replacement language, and they almost agree. Mixing them up is the most common reason a
replace "does nothing" or writes `$1` into your code.
| Tool | Group 1 | Named group | Whole match | Literal `$` or `&` |
- **Python needs raw strings.** In `"\1"` the `\1` is an escape for the character with code 1, so `re.sub`
never sees a backslash. Write `r"\1"`. Python 3.12+ warns about unknown escapes like `"\d"`; take the
- **`&` is the whole match in sed.** `s/AT&T/ATT/` is fine, but `s/ATT/AT&T/` writes `ATATTT`. Escape it: `AT\&T`.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to how its replacement says "the whole match".
steps.explain: .NET also accepts `$&`, but `$0` is what you will see in C# code. JavaScript has no `$0`: it is copied literally.

steps.prompt: A Python script wraps ids in angle brackets, but the output contains an invisible control character instead of the id. What is wrong?
options: In a normal string literal `\1` is the escape for character code 1, so `re.sub` never sees `\1`. Use raw strings: `r"<\1>"`.
Python uses `$1`, not `\1`, for groups in a replacement.
`re.sub` needs `re.compile` first, otherwise groups are not numbered.
Group numbers start at 0 in Python, so the id is `\0`.
steps.explain: Python processes string escapes before `re` gets the text. A raw string `r"..."` keeps backslashes as they are, which is why every regex and every replacement in Python should be a raw string. Python 3.12+ also prints a SyntaxWarning for the `"\d"` in the pattern.

steps.title: Rename a field, not its neighbours
prompt: The team renames the field `_log` to `_logger` across a project. A naive replace of `_log` also changes
Write the pattern and the replacement that rename only the identifier `_log`.
hints: `_` is a word character, so `\b` works on both ends of `_log`.
steps.explain: Word boundaries keep the rename to whole identifiers, and they make it idempotent: running it again changes nothing, because `_logger` has no boundary after `_log`. For a real rename in one solution, your IDE's Rename (F2 / Ctrl+R, R) is safer still: it understands scopes and strings.

steps.title: Swap two arguments
prompt: In xUnit, `Assert.Equal(expected, actual)` takes the expected value first. A test file was written the other
way round, so every failure message is backwards. Swap the two arguments of every `Assert.Equal` call whose
arguments are plain identifiers or numbers.
hints: Escape the dot and both brackets, and capture each argument with `(\w+)`.
steps.explain: Arguments like `f(x)` are left alone on purpose: a regex cannot balance nested brackets reliably. Run the simple cases with a replace, then fix the few complex ones by hand (or with an analyzer and code fix, which understands C# syntax).

steps.title: Editors: case conversion in the replace box
body: Editors add one thing the .NET replacement language lacks: **changing case** while you replace. In VS Code
(Ctrl+H, then Alt+R for regex) and in Rider's Replace with regex on, the replace box understands:
Visual Studio and ReSharper use the .NET replacement syntax (`$1`, `${name}`) and have no case conversion.
In C# code, the equivalent is a `MatchEvaluator` that calls `ToUpperInvariant()`.
> **Tip:** VS Code's "Preserve Case" button (Alt+P) keeps `Order`, `order` and `ORDER` in step when you

steps.prompt: In VS Code with regex mode on, you find `^(\w)` and replace with `\u$1` on the line `order shipped`. What is the line afterwards?
steps.explain: The match is only the first character, `o`, and `\u` upper-cases it. The rest of the line is not part of the match, so it is kept as it was. To capitalise every word, drop the `^` and use `\b(\w)`.

steps.prompt: Which tool's replacement language is each piece of syntax from?
steps.explain: When you copy a replace from a Stack Overflow answer, check which tool it was written for first. A `$<name>` from JavaScript is copied literally by .NET.

steps.title: Move usings into GlobalUsings.cs
prompt: You are moving the common `using` directives into `GlobalUsings.cs`. Turn every line of the form
Leave alone `using var` declarations, `using (...)` blocks and lines that are already global. The text has
several lines, so think about what `^` means (the **m** flag).
hints: With the **m** flag on, `^` matches at the start of every line.
steps.explain: `[\w.]+;` only accepts a dotted name followed directly by `;`, which rules out `using var x = ...` and `using (...)`. `global $0` works too: it writes `global ` and then the whole match.

steps.title: snake_case columns to PascalCase properties
prompt: You are generating C# record properties from database column names. Write `string ToPascalCase(string column)`:
upper-case the first character and every character that follows an underscore, and drop the underscores.
C# has no `\u` in replacement strings, so use `Regex.Replace` with a lambda. Use `ToUpperInvariant()`: the
result must not depend on the server's culture. `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("an internal i stays i in every culture", "IsActive", ToPascalCase("is_active"));
hints: Match the start of the string or an underscore, and capture the character after it: `(?:^|_)([a-z0-9])`.
The lambda returns `m.Groups[1].Value.ToUpperInvariant()`: the underscore is part of the match, so it disappears.
